articles.title: VW ID Buzz debuts three-row electric Microbus for the US with more power and space
articles.summary: Volkswagen revealed the long wheelbase version of its all-electric ID Buzz, which will go on sale in the US in 2024. The Microbus has a bigger battery and more power as well as ample space within for cargo or kids.
articles.body: There have been enough words typed about Volkswagen’s much-anticipated Microbus revival, the ID Buzz, so I’m just going to cut to the chase. VW unveiled the three-row, long wheelbase (LWB) version of the ID Buzz in California today — the one that will actually be coming to the US — and it’s exactly what we’ve hoped for. In addition to offering a lot more space for cargo and passengers, the US-spec Buzz has updated tech and more powerful powertrains without compromising on style. At 192.4 inches in length, the three-row ID Buzz is only 6.9 inches longer than the two-row, short wheelbase (SWB) European ID Buzz that was revealed last year, but its 127.5-inch wheelbase is 9.9 inches longer. [Image: That means the LWB ID Buzz is shorter in length than VW’s large Atlas SUV — its only current three-row offering in America — while offering a longer wheelbase and five more inches of overall height. The SWB Buzz has the same turning radius as the compact Golf hatchback despite being over a foot longer, so the LWB version should still feature similarly great maneuverability. Aside from the added length, nothing has been changed about the ID Buzz’s styling. It’s a perfect example of retro-futuristic design and easily the best execution of VW’s current design language. Unlike on the Euro Buzz we just spent two weeks with, the VW emblem on the front end of the American Buzz is illuminated, surely the largest light-up logo on any car. The available panoramic sunroof is new for the ID Buzz and is the largest in the VW Group, and it has an electrochromic tint that turns the glass from transparent to opaque. There are also some new colors and two-tone paint options, like the cabana blue you see in these photos. VW says the ID Buzz will only come with 20-inch wheels, though both smaller and bigger wheels could be available as options in the future. [Image: One potential design problem for customers lies in the rear doors. The ID Buzz gets power-sliding doors that can be opened by waving your foot under the sill, along with a power liftgate with the same tech. But unlike basically every minivan since the 2004 Toyota Sienna, the Buzz’s sliding doors don’t have windows that roll down. Instead, the Buzz has square sections of the window that powerslide backward in the vein of the original Microbus. It’s great that there is some amount of window opening — the rear windows in the SWB Buzz don’t open at all — but the area that opens isn’t nearly as big as what you get in other vans or crossovers. Increasing the wheelbase allowed VW to make some major improvements to the powertrain. The LWB ID Buzz uses a 91kWh battery pack in place of the SWB Buzz’s 82kWh pack. There’s a new electric motor at the rear that’s more powerful, putting out 282 horsepower and 406 pound-feet of torque to the rear wheels versus 201hp and 229 lb-ft in the Euro Buzz. [Image: That should result in a much quicker zero to 60mph time — the Euro Buzz does the run in about 10 seconds — and top speed has been increased from 90mph to 99mph. Available at launch will be a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive variant that will have around 330hp, though no other details have been given yet. VW also isn’t ready to say what the ID Buzz’s EPA range will be, though the larger battery and more efficient motor could give it a longer range than the 260-mile WLTP estimate of the SWB Buzz. The ID Buzz will be offered with two different seating configurations. As standard, the second row of seats is a three-person bench, giving the van seven seats in total. There is the option for a pair of captain’s chairs for the second row, too. As with the SWB ID Buzz, the seats in the second row can’t be removed, but the new two-person third-row bench can be removed completely. Both the second and third rows fold to create a flat surface — though neither set folds into the floor. And there’s an available removable cargo shelf to extend that surface area and provide storage cubbies underneath. The second row can be slid fore and aft, and the seat backs can be adjusted up to 16 degrees or fold forward for easier third-row access. All three rows of seats get their own air vents, too. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Other than the added seats and length, the design of the ID Buzz’s cabin is identical to the Euro version. The large windshield, additional quarter windows, and raised seating position provide a phenomenal view out, and the door panels have great ergonomics and armrests. The dash features a lovely faux wood panel, and each interior color scheme offers a mix of different colors and materials. (Sadly, the orange and white won’t be available in the US; instead, we’ll get a more muted gray and brown motif.) Like on the Euro Buzz, the center console is removable and features movable dividers that double as a bottle opener and ice scraper. The interior is filled with Buzz logos and little Easter eggs like smiley faces on fastener covers. One major improvement over the Euro-spec ID Buzz is the infotainment system. While the Buzz gets either a 10-inch or 12-inch touchscreen across the pond, in the US, it’s fitted with a new 12.9-inch screen as standard that’s shared with the ID.7 sedan. This new screen has an overhauled operating system that’s simpler to use and a lot more customizable, plus it finally has illuminated volume and temperature sliders. (The 5.3-inch digital gauge cluster screen looks the same as the Euro car’s.) [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: It remains to be seen how much better the updated system will actually be in practice, but anything would be an improvement over VW’s existing infotainment. The ID Buzz has eight USB-C ports throughout, including in clever locations like the door panels and the top of the windshield for a dashcam, and there’s a wireless charging pad in the dash. The ID Buzz will come with a long list of standard features. The 12-way power front seats are heated, ventilated, and have a massage function, and the second-row outboard seats are heated as well. A heated windshield, heated washer nozzles, and heated steering wheel are also included. Every ID Buzz will get 30-color ambient interior lighting, keyless entry, automatic climate control, and a suite of active safety tech with hands-on Level 2 highway assist. Options include a 14-speaker Harman Kardon audio system, a head-up display, a 360-degree camera system, and parking assist with remote parking. Volkswagen hasn’t given an exact release date yet, only saying that the three-row ID Buzz will go on sale in the US in 2024. Pricing hasn’t been announced, either, but given the amount of standard equipment and the Euro Buzz’s already high price — it starts at the equivalent of almost $60,000 in Germany — the American ID Buzz could start at around $70,000. That’s a lot of cash for sure, but the ID Buzz is truly a league of its own in terms of style and packaging. The Microbus is finally back, and it’s poised to capture the hearts of thousands of people once more.

articles.title: Rode’s all-in-one video production console is now smaller and cheaper
articles.summary: Rode’s new $499 Rodecaster Video S is a smaller and cheaper version of the Rodecaster Video portable audio and video production console it launched last year.
articles.body: Rode has announced a new version of the Rodecaster Video portable production console it launched just over a year ago, but the Rodecaster Video S isn’t a replacement. The Rodecaster Video S offers similar functionality to the original, including switching and mixing multiple video and audio sources and replacing blue or green screens, but with an even smaller footprint and price. The Rodecaster Video launched at $1,199 in late September 2024, while the new S version is available for preorder now for less than half that, at $499. The smaller version can’t accommodate as many video sources as the original, which itself was designed to be a limited but more affordable alternative to professional video switchers used in dedicated studios. At nearly $500, the Rodecaster Video S still isn’t a cheap tool for amateur streamers. But for established podcasters looking to test the waters with video versions of their content, it’s an even more affordable and accessible all-in-one solution when you factor in the built-in functionality like chroma keying and compatibility with both professional and consumer-grade audio and video gear. [Image: The smaller Rodecaster Video S has three HDMI video inputs, a USB-C port for connecting devices like webcams, and a single HDMI output. The Rodecaster Video S is powered by the same unnamed “high-performance octa-core processor” as the previous version, with video capabilities that max out at 1080p. It’s a couple inches shorter and almost 400 grams lighter, but the improved portability does come with some sacrifices. The Rodecaster Video featured four HDMI inputs, two HDMI outputs, and a pair of multifunction USB-C inputs for connecting mics and webcams. This new version has just three HDMI inputs, a single multifunction USB-C port for audio and video devices, and one HDMI video output. The Video S does carry forward the original’s pair of combo XLR/1/4” jack inputs, so it’s still compatible with professional-grade microphones, but you can alternately connect USB mics or Rode’s Series IV wireless mics using two built-in wireless receivers. A pair of 1/4” jacks provide custom mixes and levels to two sets of wired headphones, but the dedicated speaker outputs found on the original have been removed. [Image: The Rodecaster Video S includes 10 large buttons for triggering scenes and switching between video inputs, while last year’s version had 14. You’ll still find a two-inch touchscreen on the Rodecaster Video S with its own dial controller for navigating settings and making adjustments, but the number of large buttons used to switch between video sources or load up to five preset scenes configurable using Rode’s desktop app has been reduced from 14 to 10. Other features carried over from the original Rodecaster Video include livestreaming to desktop software or directly to platforms like YouTube, Twitch, and Facebook. Or you can record broadcasts, including the individual video and audio sources separately, to an external USB storage drive for editing later. And because the Rodecaster Video S is designed for smaller productions, if you don’t have the budget for a dedicated operator, the console itself can automatically switch between multiple camera angles based on who’s speaking.

articles.title: Are Meta's new smart glasses cool and useful enough to dispel the 'ick' factor?
articles.summary: Meta debuted new glasses without a camera, plus a bunch of new styles to choose from.
articles.body:
At Meta Connect on Wednesday, CEO Mark Zuckerberg introduced the company's newest hardware: a slimmed down VR headset with a brand new design, and new Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses without a camera. The audio-only glasses are lighter, weighing 43 grams, have up to 12 hours of battery life and let wearers listen to music without headphones and chat with Meta's new Muse AI agent.

Zuckerberg also revealed a new hearing enhancement feature that users can pay extra for that turns the glasses into an FDA-cleared, over-the-counter hearing aid that can compensate for perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.

"As we tested this out, it became really clear that this had the potential to be life-changing for a lot of people," he said, introducing a video with fashion designer Lindsay Jones. She described how the glasses had helped her hear better, despite gradual hearing loss in her left ear, where she said she often can't hear conversation in noisy areas.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses come in 23 colors and lens combinations and feature two new styles: one based on the Ray-Ban Clubmaster frames and a rectangular style called Burbank. The audio glasses are available for pre-order at $349 and ship Oct. 13.

Zuckerberg didn't say anything directly about the ongoing problem with Meta's line of smart glasses in his presentation, and it's likely that the launch of the audio-only glasses is the biggest response we'll get. The company's camera-toting glasses have earned a reputation as a tool for creeps who record videos of people (most often women and girls) without their consent and harass store workers for social media views . Several jurisdictions across the U.S. restrict the use of smart glasses in courthouses now, with New York imposing a ban on smart glasses in all court buildings statewide.

Meta is aware of the image its glasses have, even if it won't say the quiet part out loud. In August, the company rolled out a fix for a feature that let smart glasses users record video with the indicator light covered, potentially allowing the wearer to record others without their knowledge or permission. And in July, Instagram Head Adam Mosseri said the platform would ban users who post these harassing videos on its platform, but several news outlets have reported the videos are still accessible.

But just because Meta launched audio-only glasses doesn't mean it's doing away with camera glasses. On Wednesday, the company also unveiled the third-generation $499 Ray-Ban Meta glasses, which have improved battery life and microphones, and come in 27 color and lens combinations. The cameras on these glasses will be able to record videos with Dolby Atmos spatial audio soon, Meta says.

The company updated its lower-priced Meta Glasses as well, which debuted in June. They start at $249, with several new stylized versions: an updated Kylie Jenner-branded set and two new frames made in collaboration with Blackpink singer Lisa, each priced at $399. And Meta will sell its Ray-Ban Display glasses online in the U.S. for the first time, with a starting price of $799.

With all these hardware announcements — particularly the audio-only glasses and the plethora of new smart glasses styles — Meta is trying to make it more enticing than ever to choose a pair of smart glasses instead of regular ones. Now, potential users have the option: camera or no camera, plus a ton of fashion-forward styles that will make it hard to recognize smart glasses from basic ones.

But none of this actually addresses or fixes the creep factor and ongoing abuse of its camera glasses. Meta is still the leader in the smart glasses space, and thanks to its much lower-priced models, that's likely to continue despite competition from Snap's new Specs AR priced at $2,200 , and with Google , Apple and Samsung all expected to debut their own smart glasses.

It's possible that Zuckerberg and Meta leadership may believe that, since their smart glasses are the most popular brand by a wide margin, they don't need to directly address the privacy concerns with glasses that can record video. If Meta didn't already have such a poor privacy reputation , maybe they could get away with that. Audio-only glasses are certainly a step in the right direction, but it remains to be seen if those will be nearly as popular as the camera-carrying originals.

articles.title: Meta's Muse Charm looks like a Tamagotchi, but it's tapping into a much newer trend | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Meta’s new AI gadget may look like a Tamagotchi, but its dangling form factor taps into a much broader Gen Z trend around bag charms, retro tech, and turning gadgets into fashion accessories.
articles.body:
Is Meta’s just-announced Muse Charm a playful device that will make AI more approachable to everyday consumers, or will it be yet another flop in a long list of AI hardware gadgets that didn’t take off, like the Ai Pin, Rabbit, or Friend pendant? Reactions, so far, have been mixed. What the Charm is, however, is on-trend.

Like it or not, the form factor could potentially appeal to Gen Z consumers who, in this post- Labubu era, have already been into various dangling items from keychains and bags. It’s all part of a broader kitschy, retro-inspired shift in their approach to fashion and technology.

Already, Gen Z has created a market for things that dangle, with everything from lip glosses to hand sanitizers to sunblocks to fragrances and more turned into bag charms , primarily targeted at women.

Hailey Bieber’s viral Rhode lip case, which stuck the lip gloss onto a phone case , had a big influence on this idea that beauty products could also be fashion accessories, as did its other beauty-focused bag charms . (The brand saw $212 million in annual net sales from a lineup of roughly 10 products, Vogue noted last year, as the company announced its billion-dollar exit to Elf Beauty.)

Then there was the Labubu craze , which saw sales of the so-ugly-it’s-cute fuzzy monster bag charm explode, growing Pop Mart’s (the Chinese retailer behind the product) revenue to $1.8 billion in 2024 , a 7x jump from 2019. While demand for the Labubu itself has since faded, the concept of the decorative bag charm has not. One analyst firm estimates the global bag charm market will grow to over $1 billion by 2030 .

Today, bag charms can be characters, bedazzled beauty products, or other whimsical designs or objects, like Coach’s coveted cherry charms , a Gen Z favorite . They’ve proven popular because they’re a means of expressing your personality, just as humans have done for ages through their fashion choices, makeup, and jewelry.

Similarly, Meta’s Muse is a customizable character; you design your own avatar, which makes the AI agent a reflection of you, too.

And, as many have pointed out, Muse Charm’s form factor recalls a Tamagotchi, the pocket-sized digital virtual pet that became a major toy fad in the late 90s and again in the mid-2000s.

However, the Tamagotchi is not the most current reference. It seems the Muse Charm is actually a twist on what some young people are already doing with their Apple Watch. Often meant as a way to repurpose an older device , the concept of the Apple Watch keychain or charm has been growing in popularity, fueled by TikTok videos showing different ways to use the watch when not on your wrist.

On retailers like Amazon and Walmart, and marketplaces like eBay and Etsy , there are thousands of Apple Watch keychains, straps, pendants, lanyards, clips, and bag charm cases now available in nearly every style you can think of. As you might expect, these keychain watches are often being adopted by younger women as a fashion accessory first, rather than a piece of technology.

This all then intersects with the broader retro-tech trend , which has seen older tech like digital cameras, flip phones, iPods, CDs , cassette tapes, home phones , and wired earbuds making a quiet comeback.

This vibe shift in tech comes as young people describe the addictive, algorithm-driven feeds and “soulness” nature of technology as making them feel more disconnected, which has also fed into this trend of wanting tech they can touch and feel. (One startup, Clicks, is even bringing back the physical phone keyboard in a BlackBerry-inspired device , for instance.)

For Gen Z, these physical objects help them feel more connected with the technology they’re using and offer a sense of control over a world where technology has become so deeply integrated into our lives that it no longer feels like a choice to use it.

Young women , again, have been at the forefront of this trend, with some even crafting their own portable, mini computers, “cyberdecks, ” which they fit inside clamshell purses or custom cases, and bedazzle with jewels, flowers, stickers, pearls, and other items to make them feel more personal.

That brings us back to the Muse Charm. While it’s clearly designed with the tech-as-fashion-accessory trend in mind, that doesn’t mean it will be a hit.

Meta has abused consumer trust over the years to such an extent that it may never fully recover.

To name just a few examples: The tech giant had to settle with the FTC over charges that it deceived consumers by making users’ private information public without their consent, and has been penalized by the FTC for numerous privacy-related violations. In 2023, the FTC charged Meta with violating a privacy order that was filed after the 2019 settlement. It’s also been repeatedly hauled before Congress over its harms to minors, has lost or settled multiple lawsuits over the same topics, and has seen various whistleblowers outing its abuses.

These careless privacy practices could ultimately see Meta lose the battle to be the consumer AI of choice… unless, of course, consumers decide that the “devil you know” is better than the one you don’t. (Especially when the latter are those warning AI could put an end to the human race .)

Meta’s end game, after all, is highly-targeted, highly-personalized ads. If that’s the privacy tradeoff in gaining access to free AI — Meta said it will monetize Muse by taking a small fee from transactions — consumers could be willing to take the risk.

It’s powered by an Intel Core i7-14700KF processor, and paired with 32GB of 6000MHz DDR5 memory and an Nvidia RTX 5070 Founders Edition with 12GB of VRAM. The case is a CyberPowerPC MA-O1, an in-house design with extensive cooling options and three dedicated knobs for adjusting internal RGB lighting colors. [Product: CyberPowerPC (Core i7/RTX5070) | While it might not feel like it at first blush, this is a solid value for a gaming PC that’s ready to rock out of the box. The RTX 5070 in this machine is likely to run you upwards of $800 by itself at the moment (it launched in 2025 for $549), and 32GB of fast memory can be $400 or more. articles.title: Is everyone bricking their phone to stop doomscrolling?
articles.summary: The $59 Brick device promises to help curb phone addiction, but free iPhone and Android tools may already do the job. Here's what to try first.
articles.body: There is a funny twist to the anti-FOMO craze. Now people are worried they may be missing out on the latest way to spend less time on their phones. You may have heard people talking about "bricking" their phones. Thankfully, they are not destroying them. A $59 product called Brick is getting attention because it lets you temporarily block distracting apps and websites, creating a physical barrier between you and whatever keeps sucking you back into your screen. I understand the appeal. If you have ever picked up your phone to check one text and resurfaced 40 minutes later wondering why you were watching a stranger remodel a bathroom, you know how quickly a quick check can turn into a scroll. Still, my first reaction is this: before you buy another piece of technology to keep you away from technology, use the controls already sitting inside the phone you paid for. Apple has expanded Screen Time in iOS 27. Android already has some useful Digital Wellbeing controls. A few simple changes can also make distracting apps a little harder to reach and help break that automatic urge to grab your phone. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com. Register and receive the replay and step-by-step guide afterward. CAN TECH REALLY GET YOU OFF YOUR PHONE AND INTO REAL LIFE? More than half of Americans think they spend too much time on their phones This trend is tapping into something much bigger than one gadget. Pew Research Center surveyed 9,750 U.S. adults from May 26 through June 1, 2026. It found 53% say they spend too much time on their smartphone. Among adults ages 18 to 29, that jumps to 70%. It stands at 64% among adults ages 30 to 49, then drops to 49% among people 50 to 64 and 25% among those 65 and older. Here is another number that grabbed me: 26% of U.S. adults say they use their smartphone almost constantly. Among adults under 30, that rises to 42%. A third of adults ages 30 to 49 say the same. Think about that phrase for a second. Almost constantly. Phones help us navigate, communicate and get an incredible amount done. I certainly would not want to give mine up. The problem begins when useful turns into automatic and you find yourself opening the same app without even remembering why you picked up the phone. Plenty of people are trying to cut back Awareness is already turning into action. Pew found 45% of U.S. adults tried to cut back on smartphone use during the previous 12 months. Among adults under 50, the figure reaches 58%. Yet among people who tried cutting back, only a quarter said they were extremely or very successful. That gap tells you a lot. Knowing you want to use your phone less and actually putting it down are two different things. The problem with willpower is that your phone is always right there, and the apps fighting for your attention are only a tap away. Teens are noticing the pull too. Pew found 45% of teens say they spend too much time on social media. Forty-four percent say they have cut back on social media use, and an identical share say they have cut back on smartphone use. Your phone may also be stealing sleep The effects can follow you right into bed. Pew found 62% of adults under 30 say their smartphone hurts the amount of sleep they get. Across U.S. adults overall, 41% say their phone hurts their sleep while only 5% say it helps. I suspect plenty of us know how that happens. The phone goes on the nightstand. You check one last thing, then another notification arrives. Before long, your bedtime has moved. That is why I think the bigger lesson in this trend is making distracting apps a little harder to reach. If opening an app takes more effort, you get a moment to decide whether you really want to go there. TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS Why people are 'bricking' their phones Brick takes that idea and turns it into something physical. First, you choose which apps or websites you want to block and create different modes inside the Brick app. To start a session, tap your phone against the physical Brick. Another option lets you begin remotely by pressing and holding the virtual Brick in the app for five seconds. Getting back into those blocked apps usually requires another tap against the physical Brick. That is the part I find interesting. Leave the Brick downstairs while you work upstairs, and your easy way back into those distracting apps is suddenly in another room. The device currently costs $59 and supports iPhones running iOS 17 or later and Android devices running Android 12 or later. Head to CyberGuy.com to get 10% off the Brick with our link. One Brick can also work with multiple phones. Meanwhile, Strict Mode makes common workarounds harder, including deleting the Brick app or changing certain settings during a session. If you lose the device or cannot reach it, you get five Emergency Unbricks. I like the thinking behind it. Sometimes a physical barrier can work better than another warning on the same screen you are trying to stop staring at. Still, I would try the free controls already built into your phone before spending $59. PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US Use Screen Time to put limits on distracting apps Apple documents new Time Allowances and Screen Time Schedules in iOS 27. Apple also says all of your Apple devices need version 27 or later to use the latest Screen Time features across devices. If you do not see those newer options on your iPhone, App Limits and Downtime still give you useful ways to cut down on distracting apps. How to set an App Limit on iPhone Go to: Settings → Screen Time → App Limits → Add Limit Choose the app category you want to control. You can also tap a category to select a specific app instead. Tap Next, choose how much time you want to allow each day, then tap Done. For example, you could give yourself 30 minutes of Instagram or put a daily limit on your entire social networking category. It is a simple way to decide how much time you want to give an app before you are already deep into the scroll. Schedule time away from distracting apps If certain times of day are your weak spot, Downtime can help. Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Downtime → Scheduled Choose Every Day or Customize Days, then set when you want Downtime to start and end. During Downtime, most apps and notifications are restricted, while phone calls and apps you choose to allow remain available. You can also turn on Block at Downtime if you want the limit to be harder to ignore. OPINION: WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO You can decide which apps stay available by going to: Settings → Screen Time → Always Allowed That way, you can keep apps you genuinely need available without leaving every distracting app within easy reach. Look at your real screen-time numbers first Before setting any limits, spend a minute looking at where your time actually goes. Go to: Settings → Screen Time → Daily Average Tap Day or Week to see your usage. Scroll down to see Pickups and Notifications too. That pickup number may tell you even more than your total screen time. Maybe you spend only a few minutes at a time in an app but reach for your phone 80 times throughout the day. That tells me your challenge may be the habit of grabbing the device rather than one particular app. Start with whatever surprises you most. Use Focus to stop your iPhone from constantly pulling you back Notifications can undo all your good intentions, and you do not need Apple Intelligence to quiet them. Go to: Settings → Focus Choose a Focus such as Do Not Disturb, Personal, Sleep or Work. From there, you can decide which people and apps are allowed to interrupt you. You can also add a schedule, so Focus turns on automatically during the parts of your day when you want fewer distractions. This gets at something Screen Time alone cannot fix. Sometimes you did not decide to pick up the phone. The phone asked you to. Cutting down those invitations may be one of the easiest ways to stop checking it so often. Android has free anti-doomscrolling tools too Android phones include Digital Wellbeing tools that can show you how much time you spend in apps, how often you open them and how many notifications they send. Exact menu names can vary between Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones. On Google Pixel Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing Tap the chart to see your screen time, how often you open apps and how many notifications you receive. Set app timers Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers Next to the app you want to limit, tap Set timer , choose how much time you want to allow and tap OK . When your time runs out, the app closes and its icon dims. The timer resets at midnight. Use Focus mode Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Focus mode Choose the apps you want to pause. While Focus mode is on, you cannot use those apps and their notifications stop. Tap Turn on now to start it immediately or Set a schedule to have it turn on automatically. On Samsung Galaxy Set app timers Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App timers Tap Apps and app categories , then choose the apps or categories you want to control. Tap Add schedule , choose the days and amount of time you want to allow, then tap Save . Menu wording can vary slightly by Galaxy model and software version. Pixel can put a PIN behind your app limits On current Pixel phones, you can also protect app limits with a separate PIN. Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → App limits → App limits PIN Turn on PIN for app time limits , unlock your phone, then create and confirm a four-digit PIN. This adds another step before you can change a limit on impulse. Make your Android phone less inviting before bed On Google Pixel Go to: Settings → Digital Wellbeing → Bedtime mode → Bedtime routine Choose when Bedtime mode should turn on. You can use a schedule or have it activate while your phone is charging during certain hours. You can also customize options including Grayscale, Keep the screen dark, Dim the wallpaper and Dark theme . On Samsung Galaxy Samsung handles this through Sleep mode . Go to: Settings → Modes and Routines → Sleep Tap When to start this mode, choose Sleep schedule , then set your usual sleep and wake times. Tap Save and then Done . You can also turn on options including Do not disturb, Grayscale and Dark mode while Sleep mode is active. 6 ways to win back attention from your phone You do not need to overhaul your habits overnight. Start with your biggest distractions and make them a little harder to reach. 1) Find the apps actually stealing your time Check Screen Time on iPhone or Digital Wellbeing on Android. Look for the apps taking the biggest bite out of your day and how often you pick up or unlock your phone. Do not try to fix everything at once. Start with the biggest problem. 2) Turn off notifications you rarely need Every alert is another invitation to look at your screen. Keep the notifications that deserve immediate attention. Silence the ones that are simply trying to bring you back into an app. 3) Set limits before you start scrolling Create your limits while you are thinking clearly instead of after you have already disappeared down a feed. Use App Limits and Downtime on iPhone or App timers and Focus mode on Android. 4) Make distracting apps harder to reach Move your worst offenders off the Home Screen. Log out when you finish. If you have to search for an app and sign back in, that gives you a little time to ask yourself whether you actually wanted to open it. You are creating your own speed bump. 5) Put physical distance between you and the phone Leave it somewhere else during dinner. Put it out of reach while you work. Charge it away from the bed. This may sound almost too simple, but sometimes distance works better than another setting buried inside a menu. 6) Make your limits harder to ignore Try the free tools first. If you continually override every limit, delete every timer or find yourself reaching for the same apps anyway, then consider something stricter. That might be a stronger software blocker or a physical device such as Brick. By then, you will know exactly what problem you are paying to solve. Kurt's key takeaways Here is what gets me about this whole trend. We have reached a point where people are buying a piece of technology whose job is to keep them away from another piece of technology. That says something. I love what my phone can do. I do not want a dumb phone, and I certainly do not want to throw my smartphone in a drawer. What I want is to be the one deciding when I use it instead of reacting every time an app decides it wants me back. That is why I would start with what you already have. iPhone gives you App Limits, Downtime and Focus. Android gives you app timers and Focus mode. Your phone can also tell you exactly where your time went. Use that information. If those free controls work, you saved yourself $59. If you blow through every limit you create, Brick or another stronger blocker suddenly has a purpose beyond joining a wellness craze. For me, the real test is pretty simple: when you pick up your phone, did you decide to do it or did your phone decide for you? articles.title: Qualcomm’s new ‘Elite’ sound chip might finally deliver the Wi-Fi earbud dream
articles.summary: Also, they can power earbuds with cameras.
articles.body: What if your wireless earbuds — or audio glasses — could stream high-quality lossless audio that doesn’t cut out when you leave your phone on the bedside charger or buried in the couch? Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 is its first to integrate “micro-power Wi-Fi 6E” right into the chip, so they can connect directly to your home Wi-Fi network, and from there to the cloud. [Image: Qualcomm’s old whitepaper shows that it originally required two chips for Wi-Fi earbuds. Now, Wi-Fi is integrated into the main chip. If that sounds like a familiar promise, it’s probably because Qualcomm promised something similar back in 2023 with the “S7 Pro sound platform” and its Expanded Personal Area Network (XPAN) tech, saying that Wi-Fi earbuds can do what Bluetooth alone cannot. Namely, 24-bit 96kHz lossless audio that can’t fit into Bluetooth’s meager bandwidth. But that old 7-series platform required a separate Wi-Fi chip to give you Wi-Fi earbuds, and it seems that wasn’t a winning formula for getting makers of incredibly tiny devices to adopt the tech! In fact, we’ve only ever heard of one: Xiaomi’s 2025 Buds 5 Pro, which didn’t get a global release. [Image: Now that Wi-Fi no longer requires an extra chip, perhaps the idea can take off. Qualcomm says the Elite is also 30 percent smaller, consumes up to 40 percent less power, and has twice the AI processing capabilities of the previous gen chip, all of which should be music to device makers’ ears. So far, Qualcomm says it’s working with HP on one specific unnamed product, is “working closely with Bose,” and is “pioneering a new category of intelligent hearables” (read: earbuds with built-in cameras) with Cleer. articles.title: Microsoft is killing off the ‘Copilot Plus PC’ brand
articles.summary: What will Microsoft’s next buzzword be?
articles.body: Remember when Microsoft wanted everyone to know that “Copilot Plus PCs” were the ones to get, because those were the PCs that that’d have enough built-in AI muscle to get things done? Two and a half years later, Microsoft and Qualcomm seem to be admitting the brand is already dead. Windows Central’s Zac Bowden reports that even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. “These are not called Copilot Plus PCs,” Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrom told the publication. Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s SVP of compute and gaming, seemed to agree that the brand’s time is done, telling Bowden that computers that offer the same experiences will “probably” not use that branding anymore. It’s not surprising to me that Microsoft and its partners would back away. Back in 2024, smart minds pointed out that (almost) every PC would soon contain the basic levels of AI hardware that the brand was supposed to reflect. The flagship feature of Copilot Plus PCs, Microsoft’s Recall feature, wasn’t well received, and Microsoft took flak for constantly annoying Windows users with AI upsells, not to mention the dedicated Copilot keyboard key that you can now finally remap. Besides, Microsoft’s flagship hardware is now about to have Nvidia chips instead, which will supposedly kick off a new era of personal AI in Windows. On October 7th, when Microsoft hosts a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” I’m guessing it will have a shiny new brand to replace “Copilot Plus PC.”

articles.title: Here’s the Tesla Semi… again
articles.summary: Tesla re-launched its long-delayed Semi truck with a new list of customers who plan to use the heavy-duty EV for freight delivery.
articles.body: Remember the Tesla Semi? The long-gestating, heavy-duty truck first introduced in concept form in 2017 is finally in volume production as of April 2026 — nearly a decade after its initial introduction. On Thursday evening, the company held yet another event for the Semi to demonstrate to customers and investors that the long wait was finally over. The event was held at Tesla’s new Semi factory next to Gigafactory Nevada, where the company says it can build 50,000 trucks a year, or 1,000 per week. The purpose was to announce a raft of new (and old) customers for the Semi, including PepsiCo, US Foods, DHL, WattEV, ABF, Einride, IMC, and OK Produce. (Most of these names were leaked ahead of the event by a YouTuber flying a drone over the company’s facility in Sparks, Nevada.) First deliveries of the truck started this week. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: But there were still a lot of missing details that could have helped explain why the wait was so long, and where the Semi goes from here. Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers, nor did it update the price of the Semi — which is rumored to be $290,000 for the long range version. In short, like many Tesla events these days, this one was lacking in some key updates. The trucks were supposed to go into production in 2019 but were delayed for a variety of reasons, including the covid pandemic and a global parts shortage. Tesla delivered a handful of trucks to PepsiCo in 2022, but those units were essentially built by hand on a pilot line. Back in 2017, the company advertised a starting price of $150,000 for the 300-mile version and $180,000 for the 500-mile one. Tesla never officially updated those prices until today, but Eletrek reported earlier this year that Tesla was quoting customers $290,000 for the 500-mile range version. Tesla spent the last three years refining the Semi’s design, shaving nearly 1,000 lbs off the weight, and building out a dedicated factory next to its Gigafactory in Sparks. The company revealed the final production design in February 2026, confirming two trims: a Standard Range truck with 325 miles at full 82,000-lb gross combination weight, and a Long Range version with 500 miles of range. In April, Tesla announced that the first Semi had rolled off the line at the new facility, kicking off volume production of the long-delayed truck. Tesla CEO Elon Musk wasn’t at the event — he was in Washington, DC, attending a state dinner with President Trump and Chinese President Xi — but in a pre-recorded message, he praised the Semi as “the funnest truck to drive.” “This is really going to be a revolutionary truck,” Musk said, “that is capable of carrying the heaviest loads over very long distances. With ease of recharge, Megacharger that’s capable of a megawatt of power. This is really going to be a phenomenal truck.” [Media: Battery and engineering Much of the event was devoted to the hardware and engineering that went into the truck. Tesla’s Director of Semi Truck Engineering Dan Priestley emphasized that the 500 mile figure comes from fully loaded trucks rather than tests with a diminishing payload. Tesla Vice President of Engineering Lars Moravy said a Semi carrying a lighter load of around 60,000 pounds could potentially reach about 600 miles. The lower-range truck will have lower mass and be suited to a variety of applications, giving the company multiple Semi configurations rather than relying solely on the long-range version. Tesla claims the Semi, with its lower energy cost and far fewer parts to maintain, is cheaper to run than diesel. That’s not hard to believe with diesel prices having hit historic record highs, soaring past $6.50 a gallon in the US — nearly double what it cost a year ago. Tesla says the fully loaded truck now consumes about 1,700 Wh/mile, compared with an original target of 2,000 Wh/mile. The efficiency gains allow Tesla to use a smaller, lighter and cheaper battery while retaining the same range. The Semi is using Tesla’s in-house 4680 battery cells, replacing the purchased 2170 cells used in previous test versions. Tesla says the change, combined with vehicle-efficiency improvements, produces a lower-mass, lower-kWh battery without sacrificing range. The company has also substantially redesigned the powertrain and drive axle since the Semi’s initial reveal. The truck gets a new steel-caged rotor instead of the earlier carbon-fiber-sleeved rotor, a bar-wound stator shared with Cybertruck, and a redesigned drive axle that is about 80 kilograms lighter. Tesla also eliminated the three separate oils used in the original drive axle, leaving no oil in the hub and one common oil for the motor and gearbox, which Moravy says should last more than 250,000 miles. The hydraulic steering has been replaced by redundant electric power steering that Tesla says provides much greater precision and response. Meanwhile, the truck’s increased wheel cut gives it nearly the turning radius of a Model Y. Tesla specifically designed the system to make tight urban and loading-dock maneuvers easier, Priestley said. The Semi also shares parts with the newly road-worthy Cybercab, using the same indirect thermal system, including pumps, compressors, and heat exchangers, as the autonomous vehicle. Tesla says the system eliminates long refrigerant lines running to the front of the vehicle and can move heat between the cabin, battery and drive unit to improve efficiency. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Charging and uptime Over the past year, Tesla has been building up a customer list for the Semi, including PepsiCo, DHL, ABF Freight, and others. Autonomous trucking startup Einride announced a 500-truck order in August, while IMC Logistics said it would buy 50 Semis for California drayage earlier this week. And on Monday, Tesla was selected by “a coalition of the world’s largest cargo-owning shippers” to supply 2,500 trucks for zero-emission freight shipping in California. Now the challenge will meeting this demand by getting trucks to customers — and quickly. Some of these freight operators have been waiting for years for Tesla to deliver its promised electric trucks, and any more delay will just further damage the company’s reputation. "“This is really going to be a revolutionary truck.”" - Elon Musk Charging will be another challenge, as the Semi requires higher power levels in order to fill its enormous 822 kWh battery pack. Tesla has begun to build out its Megacharger system that can deliver up to 1.2 Megawatts of power per stall. Tesla says it will have more than 30 Semi charging stations representing over 200 megawatt-capable posts by the end of the year, while also supporting customer-installed overnight charging. During the event, Priestley and Moravy kept checking in on a Semi charging at one of the new Megawatt chargers, demonstrating a 3-60 percent charge in about 30 minutes. Tesla is positioning the Semi as an integrated fleet product, not just an electric truck. The company says its existing fleet has demonstrated more than 98 percent uptime, compared to an average 90-95 percent for diesel-powered class 8 trucks across the industry. Tesla is also building out a dedicated Semi service, mobile service, remote diagnostics and OTA updates around the truck. The executives demonstrated a number of innovations they said would make for a better driving experience, including driver profiles that follow drivers from truck to truck and range estimates dynamically accounting for changing payloads. While Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers or starting prices, Musk did say that the “waiting list is significant” and encouraged people to place orders. The company repeatedly emphasized how the Semi is able to achieve a lower total cost of ownership versus diesel, including lower energy costs, reduced maintenance, and less exposure to diesel-price volatility. “You know, volatility in the oil market and the diesel market goes up and down,” Moravy said. “But typically, we’ve seen in the history of the last 20 years, electricity is pretty flat. And wouldn’t it be great to have a flat cost in your shipping rates?” Images by Tesla

articles.title: Budget phones are disappearing fast, report says by 2030, 40% of sub-Rs 20,000 smartphones may be gone
articles.summary: The era of the budget smartphones is rapidly shrinking.
articles.body: The era of the budget smartphones is rapidly shrinking. Over 230 million annual smartphone shipments priced below $200 (Rs 20,000) will vanish from worldwide retail channels between 2025 and 2030, a report has said. According to Counterpoint Research’s Smartphone Shipment Forecast by Price Band tracker, this segment will contract by roughly 40% through the end of the decade. The decline comes even as total worldwide smartphone shipments stage a broader rebound back toward 2025 volumes.Why budget phones’ shipment will squeezeThe disappearing budget tier stems largely from structural aftershocks linked to the 2026–2027 industry downturn. A combination of rising prices for mobile chipsets and memory, higher baseline hardware requirements and phone makers scaling back unprofitable market footprints has made entry-level devices increasingly hard to sustain, the report said, adding, as components eat up a far larger share of total build costs on inexpensive devices, manufacturers have virtually no room to absorb price jumps.It also said that rather than buying brand-new budget handsets, consumers are responding in several ways. For example, users are delaying upgrades and extending how long they keep their existing devices. Some buyers are turning to certified refurbished and second-hand phones, and a portion of buyers is moving up into higher price tiers via installment plans.“The smartphone market will recover in unit terms, but the affordable segment will not return to its previous standing. The opportunity now shifts toward better-specced mainstream devices and premium products, although higher tiers cannot absorb all the lost volume. The result will be a market that is similar in overall size but materially different in value and competitive profile. There is also a wider connectivity risk, as the loss of affordable new smartphones could make it harder for first-time users in lower-income markets to come online,” said Yang Wang, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.Smartphone shipment rebound expected through 2030Counterpoint estimates that overall smartphone deliveries will climb back to approximately 1.20 billion units by 2030, just behind 2025 benchmark levels. The stagnation across the mid-range highlights that budget volume is not simply flowing upward in a straight line. Instead, delayed purchase cycles and disappearing first-time buyer demand mean higher tiers will not make up for all the lost volume under $200.Across developing and lower-income markets, device affordability remains the single greatest roadblock to mobile internet access. As sub-$200 options disappear, the transition from basic feature phones or shared family devices to personal smartphone ownership risks slowing to a crawl. This slowdown threatens to complicate long-term efforts by network operators, software developers, and governments seeking to broaden digital public infrastructure, localized content and mobile financial services.You use AI every day. articles.title: Insta360 conquered 360 cameras — now it’s eyeing glasses
articles.summary: Insta360 has 73 percent of the 360 camera market. What’s next?
articles.body: It’s right there in the name: “Insta360” makes 360-degree cameras, ones that film every angle simultaneously so you can shoot first and frame later. It didn’t invent the idea, but Insta360 has become so synonymous with 360 cameras that it dominates the category with 73 percent of worldwide marketshare. It’s preparing to ship so many cameras, it just spent $298 million — more than GoPro’s entire valuation — on memory chips alone. But as Insta360 sells its 10 millionth camera and opens its first flagship US store in New York City’s Times Square, it’s thinking bigger than two hemispherical lenses on a stick. It’s looking to challenge Canon, Sony, Nikon, and Fujifilm by becoming a “top imaging camera company” or “even a tech company,” cofounder Max Richter tells me — and it’s experimentally building its own mirrorless cameras and smart glasses to get there. Insta360, also known as Shadow Stone or Arashi Vision in its native China, isn’t targeting Meta’s AI glasses or DSLR-wielding professional photographers just yet. Nor is it trying to replace the smartphone camera in your pocket. [Image: The Insta360 X6, on a selfie stick. “We don’t try to fight against the rise of the smartphone in photography and content creation,” says Richter. “We see that there’s an opportunity between smartphone users and professional cameras — a growing trend that people want to express themselves,” he adds. He tells me that if Insta360 were to sell a pair of smart glasses, “we wouldn’t necessarily compete with companies on smart intelligent features.” It’d be about helping people conveniently capture high-quality images, not about an AI assistant on your face. And while that doesn’t sidestep the “pervert glasses” problem, there might be room for Insta360 to go about it differently, with headgear that’s obviously a camera instead of covertly spying. Though Insta360’s smart glasses ambitions haven’t been widely reported — I could only find one brief mention — founder JK Liu previously confirmed that two mirrorless cameras are already in development. One will have a shape that “you have never thought of before,” Liu told MyNavi News in August. (Liu reportedly became a billionaire when Insta360 went public last year.) “When you think about mirrorless, for us it would really go into making it more convenient and making a camera that is really suited for a new generation of content creators, not necessarily what’s already out there on the market,” Richter tells The Verge. If Insta360 does expand into those camera categories, they’ll just be the tip of the spear. The company has already been pushing into many other categories dominated by its Chinese rival DJI, including DJI-challenging drones, gimbals and gimbaled baby steadycams, and modular action cameras. [Image: Insta360’s current camera lineup, not counting its drone and professional VR rigs. While Insta360 might be the 360-camera market leader with 73 percent share, it’s a distant number 2 in other categories that DJI serves. IDC estimates that Insta360 has 20 percent of the worldwide handheld smart camera market compared to DJI’s 73 percent overall. Still, Insta360 is making significant headway: In Q2 2026, it had 43 percent of the detachable action camera market, 17 percent of non-detachable GoPro style action cameras, and its brand-new Luna Ultra already has 6 percent marketshare in gimbaled cameras. GoPro itself, meanwhile, is a distant number 3 in IDC data, with just 3 percent of the smart camera market in Q2 2026, after shipments fell by half to just 200,000 cameras in the quarter. It’s not unthinkable that Insta360 could help challenge traditional cameras. The traditional market leader, Canon, shipped 4.5 million digital cameras last year according to Nikkei data. DJI shipped 4.3 million cameras last quarter alone, according to IDC. [Image: [Image: Insta360’s founders have explained that their grand vision is to become the robot cameraman for the world — not necessarily an actual humanoid robot, but rather an expectation that these devices can do more and more of the capture and motion and editing themselves, automatically understanding your intent using built-in AI tech. The company’s latest Insta360 X6 is another small step in this direction: It comes with an onboard AI model and enough processing to automatically create a highlight reel from your footage while the camera is plugged in and charging, and it’s got a 2.0 version of a previous “InstaFrame” feature that can track and frame the person you select and automatically produce a video. Insta360’s also launching a new feature for the X6 that can create 3D Gaussian splats with one tap in the company’s smartphone app, for free. It takes an hour or two for cloud servers to process the video, and users will only get four free splats per month, says Insta360 spokesperson Caroline Chen, but early results look neat. It’s not at all clear whether the United States will embrace Insta360 the way Insta360 has embraced the US. While Apple, Best Buy, and Costco all stock the company’s products, that could change if the US government decides to enact a foreign camera ban — or if it simply decides that Insta360 is a drone company, like DJI, and pushes back on its cameras, too. [Image: Insta360 technically already has a headset — it comes with the Antigravity A1 drone. Insta360 already distanced itself from its drone brand Antigravity in the lead-up to the US drone ban, which will theoretically prevent Antigravity from shipping any future drones into the United States. Its first drone beat the ban by weeks. As for Insta360, “We remain on the ground,” Richter tells me. “When it comes to drones, it’s not something that Insta360 is working on,” he says, suggesting I speak to Antigravity CEO Michael Shabun instead. Richter says he’s “quite confident” that he can continue to bring cameras to people all around the world, and that Insta360 will fully comply with any local laws, but admits “there are certain things that are out of our control.” I ask: Would Insta360 consider hedging against future risk by manufacturing some products in the US? If the company was required to, perhaps — but there’s no current plan to do so. “We would potentially look into it, but it’s not in our plan or roadmap at this moment.” He says the US is a key market, and Insta360 plans to be there for the long haul.

articles.title: Meadow lets you leave your smartphone at home without sacrificing the essentials | TechCrunch
articles.summary: “We’re not Luddites... it’s just we don’t want social media, browsing, and that kind of stuff," said 25-year-old founder Shreyas Narlanka.
articles.body:
I held my breath as I walked into the concert venue and showed the bouncer a ticket barcode on a three-inch, square screen.

“If it doesn’t go through, I can try something else,” I said quickly, worried that the barcode wouldn’t work. But just as Meadow founder Shreyas Narlanka promised me, the code I scanned onto the startup’s minimalist phone earlier that day worked fine.

“Cool phone,” the bouncer said, ushering me inside.

I’d done it. With Meadow’s bare-bones smartphone, I had called an Uber, streamed Apple Music during the ride, and entered the show. Not once did I need to touch my iPhone, which I only brought with me as a backup in case the ticket scan didn’t work.

“With so many dumb phones, the Brick , and everything, the messaging is like, ‘Slow down, focus on your work’ or whatever,” Narlanka says, explaining why his company chose to build a minimal phone. “But the reason we’re different is because we’re all about getting outside and unplugging and having a sick social life.”

Go online, and you’ll see a growing mass of content and comments from people across the world feeling suffocated by being constantly connected via their smartphones and social media feeds. That’s resulting in a new device category that promises a reprieve. Some of these devices, like the Light Phone , require users to completely give up their smartphone and switch to a simpler device. Others, like the Wisephone , offer a modern touchscreen device with a minimal UI and a few apps. Still others are embracing more tactile form factors, like the Commodore Callback , which is a flip-phone with a touchscreen.

Meadow, meanwhile, is taking the middle road, intending to simply supplement your existing device. It runs Android, and so supports apps like Maps, Strava, Uber, Apple Music, and Spotify. It also has native apps for utilities like the camera, voice memos, notes, camera, text, calling, location sharing, and ticket scanning. It also supports Bluetooth, and you can connect 3.5mm headphones to it using a USB-C-to-3.5mm adapter.

“I knew there were going to be times where I needed my phone,” Narlanka said. “I didn’t want a full replacement.”

You can’t make calls and send texts with your usual phone number, though — you’ll have to set up a new plan through a subscription plan with Meadow, which gives you a separate number to use while you’re on the go.

Narlanka recommends his customers take advantage of the iPhone’s “driving” focus feature, which by default tells your top contacts that you’re on the road — instead, he says, you can customize the text to say you’re out with the Meadow. This way, you might miss the latest chatter in your group chats, but if anyone needs to contact you urgently, they’ll still be able to reach you.

“We’re not Luddites that are going to be like, ‘Streaming’s bad, and this is bad,’” he said. “It’s just we don’t want social media, browsing and that kind of stuff.”

This sentiment has become an increasingly common one. People talk about reducing their screen time as something that’s universally assumed to be good for you, like eating vegetables or flossing. Even ADÉLA , the artist whose concert I attended, used her manager’s phone to publish a celebration post after her debut album hit No. 4 on the Billboard charts.

“I have deleted social media because i want to stay sane!” the 22-year-old pop star wrote on Instagram.

Her fans don’t feel the same way — I saw several people recording the entire show on their iPhones. (There’s nothing wrong with snapping a few photos or a short video for Instagram, but an entire show?)

Speaking of cameras, the one on the Meadow worked well when out and about during the day, but the pictures weren’t great when I tried using it to take photos at the concert.

The camera app also works differently from your usual smartphone fare: You can take as many photos and videos as you want, but you can only see your photos once you get home and use the Meadow app from your main smartphone. And instead of a front-facing camera, Meadow has a tiny mirror beside the camera lens so that you can make sure you’re in the frame of your selfies.

The screen brightness and battery weren’t an issue when taking the Meadow around — if anything, the display can sometimes be a bit too bright in low-lit areas, but that meant it was always very visible outdoors.

In your hand, the small, square device feels a bit unfamiliar, though it does feel functional enough. This isn’t a device that Meadow wants you to use constantly, so it’s not a problem that it feels less comfortable than an iPhone.

Meadow is still new; it’s only shipped its first bulk batch to preorder customers so far. I ran into some small issues, too, like a glitch that showed my Uber ride had not ended for a while after I left the car (for a second I worried I had accidentally ordered a second Uber). Narlanka tells me, though, that this bug has been fixed now.

Overall, if you can handle the discomfort of managing a second phone number, Meadow works well as a device that helps you disconnect without leaving you fully off the grid.

Though Narlanka is only 25-years-old, Meadow isn’t his first startup. He dropped out of UC San Diego in 2020 when his last company, Scoutapp AI, started gaining traction. The inventory management platform for online businesses ended up being acquired by fashion resale platform StockX .

Meadow is Narlanka’s first attempt at making hardware, though his previous success has earned him backing from investors. The company raised funding in December 2024, led by Alana Goyal of basecase capital . Angel investors Terrence Rohan, Discord’s founding CMO Eros Resmini, Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch, and Diagram founder Jordan Singer also participated.

articles.title: Cricut’s new compact crafter prints, cuts, and laminates stickers
articles.summary: Cricut’s new StickerPix line are some of its smallest crafting machines and the first that don’t require a separate printer.
articles.body: Cricut announced its first crafting machines with printing capabilities that are primarily designed as all-in-one solutions for turning photos and other images into precut stickers. The Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut and Cricut StickerPix Print are also two of the smallest machines in the company’s current lineup and seem ideal for those whose crafting aspirations may be limited by their available storage space. [Image: The larger Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut prints, laminates, and cuts stickers but leaves them on the larger for easier peeling. Starting at $299, the Cricut StickerPix Print plus Cut is the larger and more expensive of the two new machines and is also available as part of pricier bundles that include more consumables. It’s compatible with 4x7-inch sticker sheets and 4x6-inch photo paper and uses a dye-sublimation printing process that relies on heat instead of spraying ink for better color reproduction. Unlike Cricut’s larger crafting machines, these new offerings include a built-in lamination process making prints resistant to water, scratches, and fading over time. [Image: The smaller and cheaper Cricut StickerPix Print lacks cutting abilities and relies on precut sticker sheets. The smaller Cricut StickerPix Print starts at $169 and is also available as part of larger bundles. It carries forward most of the functionality of the larger model but without cutting capabilities. It instead prints directly to precut sticker sheets with shapes that include circles, rectangles, and squares, but it can also be used to print 4x6 photos. The biggest difference between the StickerPix Print plus Cut and Cricut’s larger machines is that it’s only capable of cutting through the top layer of a print, producing what are known as kiss-cut stickers that come out still attached to a larger sheet. Cricut’s other machines are capable of making die-cut stickers that are sliced right through the backing paper.

articles.title: Donald Trump’s Aide Natalie Harp Switches Sides To ‘Serve’ Jimmy Kimmel in New Skit

articles.body:
The fake Harp character on Jimmy Kimmel Live! carried a golf set, briefcase, and laptop, declaring her intense devotion to Kimmel and offering to serve him, before being escorted offstage by Guillermo.

The sketch drew from real reporting about Harp’s support for Trump, her role as his executive assistant, and her nickname as a “human printer” for printing favorable articles about the president.

Jimmy Kimmel used a parody version of Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp during his Thursday monologue, turning her reported devotion to the president into a late-night comedy bit.

The woman who appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live! was not Harp herself. A doppelgänger played "Natalie Harp 2.0" and acted as Kimmel's intensely devoted assistant throughout the sketch.

Jimmy Kimmel takes a dig at Donald Trump with the help of Natalie Harp 2.0

The Jimmy Kimmel Donald Trump skit began when the fake Harp walked onstage carrying a golf set, briefcase and laptop. She called Kimmel her "guardian and protector" and removed lint from his suit.

The impersonator also offered to post "Truths" for Kimmel and repeatedly insisted that she wanted to "serve" him. Kimmel rejected her offers and eventually asked Guillermo to take her backstage.

As per The Daily Beast , the character then protested the decision.

"I can't see you backstage!" she said. "I can't hear you backstage. I cannot smell you backstage. I can't wipe you backstage. I'm here to serve you."

She also declared, "Your wife doesn't deserve you!" before the bit ended with laughter and applause from the audience.

The Jimmy Kimmel Natalie Harp parody drew from reporting about the real White House aide's relationship with Trump. The Daily Beast reported that Harp had supported Trump since 2019 and served as his executive assistant after he returned to office in 2025. The outlet also described her as a frequent presence near the president.

The source further reported that Harp had earned the nickname "human printer" for printing favorable articles about Trump. It also previously published letters attributed to Harp in which she referred to Trump as her "Guardian and Protector in this life."

"I never want to bring you anything but joy," one letter read. "You are all that matters to me. I don't want to ever let you down."

Kimmel's sketch borrowed those reported details and exaggerated them through the fictional "Natalie Harp 2.0," rather than featuring the real Natalie Harp herself.

articles.title: Leaks reveal a new Apple HomePod mini, iPad mini, and Apple TV 4K
articles.summary: New leaks found in Apple’s code reveal some of the upgrades coming to Apple’s next HomePod mini, iPad mini, and the Apple TV box.
articles.body: Apple is expected to announce more hardware before the end of the year following the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone Duo earlier this month. The updated products will include a new version of the HomePod mini, the iPad mini 8, and the Apple TV 4K, according to details and images discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris. Details from the leaks are sparse, but the HomePod Mini 2 will carry forward a similar design to the original model that debuted in late 2020. While the current model is available in bright color options including orange, yellow, and blue, the leaked images of the HomePod Mini 2 reveal new green, pink, blue, white, and black shades that are more subdued and better suited to blending into existing decor. The new iPad mini 8 will replace the seventh-generation model that launched two years ago with an upgrade from Apple’s A17 Pro chip to the recently announced A20 Pro found in the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The leaked images only show the front of the iPad mini 8, but Apple has moved its front-facing camera to the landscape edge of the tablet, while a groove on the top edge of the display, similar to the iPhone’s, seems to indicate an added speaker. As previously reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the next version of the iPad could also include improved waterproofing thanks to a new vibration-based speaker, and an OLED display like the larger iPad Pro features. The current version of the Apple TV is nearly four years old, but today’s leaks don’t give much away about what upgrades the new 4th generation version will include aside from a very similar design to its predecessor. Previous details uncovered by MacRumors’ Perris include a potential upgrade to Apple’s A17 Pro chip, while in 2024 Mark Gurman said the next Apple TV would use Apple’s in-house Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chip we now know as the N1.

articles.title: Tesla’s Optimus robot is going through growing pains
articles.summary: Tesla is reportedly running into manufacturing issues with Optimus, especially the robot’s hands, as it tries to ramp up production.
articles.body: Hitting its goal of making 20,000 Optimus robots per week is reportedly proving tricky for Tesla. The Information reports that Tesla produced “several hundred robots a week” last month, after it repurposed its Model S and Model X production lines for Optimus earlier this year. However, this strategy is reportedly creating manufacturing snags, like issues lining up parts precisely, as The Information notes: “Not only are the Optimus production lines new, but the Optimus parts are much smaller and have to fit together far more precisely than car parts.” It reports that even in the “V3” Optimus robots it’s currently producing, the hands and forearms “have more than 100 screws and other small components that currently require a worker to assemble manually.” These robots are lighter and have more cameras than previous versions, but lack a “sensing glove” currently in development that will improve durability by making it easier to replace touch sensors without swapping out the entire hand. Optimus has faced delays for years now, even as Tesla CEO Elon Musk has made bold promises about it, saying Optimus will be Tesla’s “biggest product of all time.” However, at the moment they’re still being used internally for specific tasks in limited areas, and not generally or with remote teleoperation. Tesla also reportedly plans to lease the robots initially rather than selling them, and use the training data collected to improve the robots, but it will have to get them out in the world first. Meanwhile, other developers have begun shifting to less lifelike designs for their robots, and earlier this month, Chinese regulators reportedly started holding back IPO listings for humanoid robotics companies.

articles.title: These camera apps give you more control over the iPhone 18 Pro’s aperture
articles.summary: Third-party camera apps from Moment and Blackmagic Design let you more precisely dial in an aperture setting on the iPhone 18 Pro.
articles.body: One of the questionable limitations of the iPhone 18 Pro’s new main camera with a variable aperture is that you’re limited to just four settings in the native iOS’ camera app in manual mode: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. Those same limitations are also in place when the app is adjusting the iris itself in Auto aperture mode, but it turns out that’s not a strict limitation of the iPhone’s camera hardware. Apple’s SDK allows third-party camera apps to implement more granular control of the aperture. BlackMagic Design’s well-featured and still completely free BlackMagic Camera app for iOS was one of the first third-party options to introduce support for the iPhone 18 Pro’s adjustable aperture. But instead of just four stop settings, the app offers 10 presets with additional options in-between the settings available in iOS’ camera. The iPhoneographers YouTube channel tested the new functionality in version 3.5 of the app last week and while they describe it as “pretty buggy” the app has since been updated to version 3.5.1 with “general performance and stability improvements.” Yesterday, Moment followed suit with an announcement on X that its $12.99 Moment Pro Camera II app has also been updated to support the iPhone 18 Pro’s variable aperture. You can adjust the aperture from f/1.48 to f/4.0 in 1/3 stop increments giving you 10 presets like Blackmagic’s app, which is the same approach as most digital cameras take. Given the small sensor size of the iPhone 18 Pro you may be hard-pressed to see a difference in background blur and focus depth when comparing photos with f-stops different by just 1/3 of a stop, but more control is never a bad thing.
